7.1.summary:
Bad behaviour is nothing new. Whatever wrong you run into today, you have seen its like many times before, and so has every age: the old histories, the recent ones and the streets of your own city are full of the same things.

Marcus finds this calming rather than depressing. If nothing is truly new, nothing needs to shock you, and since everything is also short-lived, nothing needs to overwhelm you either.
7.1.today: When the news cycle serves up another scandal, or a colleague pulls the same trick someone pulled at your last job, it can help to think: I know this one. It's an old story in new clothes, and it will pass like the others did.

7.2.summary:
Your principles only die if you stop thinking about them, and keeping them alive is up to you, like fanning a fire. Marcus reminds himself that he can always form the right view of things, and that events outside his mind have no direct grip on it, so being disturbed is something he lets happen.

The hopeful part is the end: you can get your life back at any time simply by looking at things again the way you did when you saw them clearly.
7.2.today: After a rough few weeks of skipped habits and short temper, you don't need a grand reset. Rereading the notes, book or advice that once steadied you, and looking at your situation through it again, is often enough to find your footing.

7.3.summary:
Much of human life looks like a show: parades and plays, animals squabbling over scraps, ants hauling loads, mice scurrying, puppets on strings. Marcus isn't sneering. He tells himself to move through all this with good humour rather than superiority.

The sting is in the last line: a person is worth about as much as the things they spend themselves on. If you chase trivia, that is your measure.
7.3.today: Watching people fight over a parking space, or a group chat erupt over nothing, it's easy to feel above it all. The better response is a smile, and then a quiet look at what you yourself spend your hours and energy on.

7.4.summary: Pay real attention. When someone speaks, notice what they're actually driving at; when something is done, look at what it really amounts to. Marcus is training himself not to take words and actions at face value but to see their purpose and meaning.
7.4.today: In a meeting, it's worth asking what a colleague's suggestion is really for rather than reacting to how it was phrased. With a friend's offhand remark, listening for what they mean usually gets you further than answering the literal words.

7.5.summary:
Ask honestly whether you're up to the task. If you are, get on with it, treating your mind as a tool nature gave you for the job. If you aren't, either hand it to someone better suited, unless duty says otherwise, or do your best with the help of someone who can fill the gap.

What matters is not who gets the credit but that the work serves the common good.
7.5.today: A manager who knows a project is beyond their expertise can pass it to a colleague who knows it better, or bring that person in alongside, instead of struggling on out of pride. The same goes for a parent asking for help with homework they can't follow.

7.6.summary: Fame doesn't last. Many people who were once celebrated have been completely forgotten, and the people who did the celebrating are long dead too. Marcus is reminding himself that renown is a poor thing to stake a life on.

7.7.summary: There's no shame in needing help. Marcus pictures a soldier storming a city wall: the job is to get over the battlements, and if you're lame and need a hand to climb, you take it. Your duty is the task itself, not proving you did it alone.
7.7.today: Asking a colleague to check your work, letting a friend help you move house, or admitting to your GP that you can't manage on your own are all ways of doing the job properly, not signs of weakness.

7.8.summary: Don't let the future unsettle you. If you get there, you'll bring with you the same reason and judgement you're using right now on the present. You already have the tools; you don't need to fight tomorrow's battles today.
7.8.today: Lying awake rehearsing next week's difficult conversation or a possible redundancy rarely helps. You will face it, if it comes, with the same good sense you're using today on today's problems.

7.9.summary:
Everything is connected, and Marcus calls that bond sacred. The universe is one ordered whole: one world made of everything, one divine power running through it, one underlying stuff, one law, and one shared reason in every thinking being.

This is the Stoic picture of the cosmos as a single living system. For Marcus it means no person or event is really separate from you, and that all reasoning beings are bound by the same truth.

7.10.summary: Everything physical soon dissolves back into the material of the universe, every pattern or form is soon absorbed back into the reason that runs it, and every memory is soon buried by time. Marcus is setting out, plainly, how short-lived everything is, himself included.

7.11.summary: For a reasoning being, acting according to nature and acting according to reason are the same thing. Stoics held that what makes humans distinctive is their capacity to reason, so living well as a human simply means living by good reason.

7.12.summary: Stand straight on your own, or be propped up by others. Marcus is telling himself that it's better to be good from your own character than to need correcting, but that if he does go wrong, he should accept being set right.

7.13.summary:
Reasoning people are like the limbs of one body: separate, but made to work together. Marcus plays on a pun in Greek, where changing one letter turns "limb" (melos) into "part" (meros). If you think of yourself merely as a part, you're still doing good out of duty or politeness.

If you feel yourself to be a limb, a living member of the whole, you love people from the heart, and doing good becomes a pleasure in itself, because it is also doing good to yourself.
7.13.today: There's a difference between helping out at the school fair because you'll be judged if you don't and helping because you genuinely feel part of the community. The second kind of help tends to be warmer, and it doesn't leave you keeping score.

7.14.summary: Let whatever happens fall on the parts of you that can feel it, and let them complain if they want. Marcus means the body and the outer circumstances. He himself, his mind, isn't harmed unless he judges that what happened is bad, and that judgement is in his power to withhold.
7.14.today: A cancelled train or a rainy holiday will bother your body and your plans. Whether it ruins your day depends on the story you then tell yourself about it.

7.15.summary: Whatever anyone else does or says, your job is to be good. Marcus pictures an emerald saying, whatever happens around me, I must be emerald and keep my colour. Goodness is your nature, not a response to how others behave, so other people's conduct is no excuse to lose it.
7.15.today: When a customer is rude, or a relative is being impossible at a family gathering, you can stay courteous and kind, not because they've earned it but because that's who you are.

7.16.summary:
Your mind doesn't frighten or hurt itself; only its own judgements do that. If something outside tries to frighten it, let it try. The body may suffer and say so, but the mind, which decides what it thinks about fear and pain, need not join in.

On its own the mind needs nothing unless it invents a need. So it stays calm and unobstructed as long as it doesn't trip itself up.

7.17.summary:
The Greek word for happiness, eudaimonia, literally means having a good daimon, a good guiding spirit within. Marcus uses the pun to scold an unwelcome thought or mental image that keeps intruding. He tells it, without anger, to leave the way it came.

It's a small, human scene: a stray impression returning out of old habit, and Marcus calmly declining to entertain it rather than fighting it.
7.17.today: When the old worry, the jealous comparison or the craving for something you've given up drifts back in, you don't need to get angry with yourself. Notice it, recognise the familiar visitor, and politely show it out.

7.18.summary:
Why fear change, when nothing at all can happen without it? Wood has to change to heat your bath, food has to change to nourish you, and nothing useful happens otherwise. The universe runs on change and likes it best.

Marcus draws the obvious, hard conclusion: your own change, including ageing and death, is just as natural and just as necessary to the way things work.
7.18.today: A new manager, children leaving home, a body that no longer does what it used to: all unsettling, yet they're the same process that gives you a cooked meal and a warm house. Nothing you value would exist without things changing.

7.19.summary:
All bodies are swept through the stuff of the universe like a torrent, each working together with the whole the way the parts of your body do. Time has already swallowed many a Chrysippus, Socrates and Epictetus.

Chrysippus was one of the great early heads of the Stoic school, and Epictetus was the former slave whose Stoic teaching shaped Marcus deeply. If even they are gone, so is every person and thing, and so will you be.

7.20.summary: Only one thing worries Marcus: that he might do something human nature doesn't allow, or do it in the wrong way, or at the wrong time. Everything else, from pain to loss to other people's behaviour, he tries to leave unworried about. His only real concern is acting badly himself.

7.21.summary: Soon you will have forgotten everything, and soon everyone will have forgotten you. Marcus states it in two flat lines. It's meant to loosen your grip on reputation and on the things that seem so pressing today.

7.22.summary: Loving even those who wrong you is a distinctly human ability. It comes easier when you remember that they're your kin, that they act out of ignorance rather than choice, that you'll both be dead soon, and above all that they haven't actually harmed you, because they haven't made your own mind or character any worse.
7.22.today: When a neighbour plays loud music late or someone cuts you off on the motorway, try running through the list: they're a person like me, they probably don't realise, we'll both be gone one day, and my own character is untouched.

7.23.summary: Nature works with the stuff of the universe like wax: it moulds a horse, breaks it up, uses the material for a tree, then a person, then something else. Each lasts only briefly. Marcus adds that there's no hardship for the thing in being broken up, any more than there was in being put together. Death is simply nature reusing the material.

7.24.summary:
A habitual scowl goes against nature. Wear it often enough and the good in your face dies away until it can't be rekindled. Marcus takes this as evidence that bad temper is contrary to reason.

He ends bluntly: if you lose even the awareness that you're doing wrong, what is left to live for? The real danger is a sour mood hardening into who you are.
7.24.today: Think of the person whose resting expression has become permanent irritation, or the habit of sighing at every request at work. Grumpiness practised daily stops being a mood and becomes a face.

7.25.summary: Nature, which runs the whole, will soon transform everything you see, making new things out of their material, and newer things out of those, so the world stays forever fresh. Marcus finds this constant renewal not sad but part of how the universe keeps itself alive.

7.26.summary:
When someone wrongs you, ask straight away what they thought was good or bad that led them to it. Once you see it, you'll pity them rather than be shocked or angry.

Either you share their idea of what's good, in which case you should forgive them, since you might have done the same, or you don't share it, in which case it's even easier to be kind to someone who has simply got things wrong.
7.26.today: A colleague who undercuts you to win a promotion probably thinks status is everything. You might once have thought the same, or still half do, so understanding rather than fury is the fairer response.

7.27.summary:
Think less about what you lack and more about what you have. Pick out the best of your possessions and imagine how much you would long for them if they were gone.

But Marcus adds a Stoic caution: don't come to treasure them so much that losing them would knock you off balance. Gratitude, yes; dependence, no.
7.27.today: Before wishing for a bigger flat or a newer car, picture losing the home or the health you already have. Then enjoy them, while remembering that they're on loan.

7.28.summary: Withdraw into yourself. Your reasoning mind has the happy quality of being content with itself whenever it acts justly, and that contentment is where peace of mind comes from. You don't need outside approval to feel settled.

7.29.summary: A string of quick commands Marcus gives himself: stop the runaway imagination, stop being jerked about by impulses like a puppet, stay in the present, understand what's actually happening to you or to others, break things down into what they're made of and what makes them what they are, think of your last hour, and leave a wrong where it was done rather than carrying it with you.
7.29.today: Being jerked about by strings looks like reaching for your phone at every buzz. Leaving the wrong where it was done means not replaying a rude email on the drive home and over dinner.

7.30.summary: Pay attention to what's said, and let your mind get properly inside what's being done and who is doing it. It's a short reminder to engage fully with the people and events in front of you instead of half-listening.

7.31.summary:
Marcus lists what to wear as your ornaments: simplicity, modesty, and indifference to everything that lies between virtue and vice, meaning things like money, health and reputation. Love people and follow God.

He then recalls an earlier writer's line that everything is governed by law, and decides that remembering this is enough. The world runs by its own order, and that's sufficient to steady him.

7.32.summary: On death: whether it means being scattered, broken into atoms, or simply ceasing to exist, it is either an ending or a change. Marcus doesn't claim to know which. His point is that neither possibility is something to dread.

7.33.summary:
On pain: pain that is truly unbearable ends quickly, by carrying us off; pain that lasts is therefore bearable. Meanwhile the mind can keep its calm by withdrawing into itself, and your judgement isn't damaged.

As for the parts of the body that hurt, let them speak for themselves if they can. Marcus, who suffered from poor health, is coaching himself through real discomfort.
7.33.today: With a long-term back problem or a migraine that drags on, it can help to notice that you are, in fact, bearing it, and that your thinking and your kindness to others don't have to suffer along with your body.

7.34.summary: On fame: look closely at the minds of people who crave it, at what they avoid and what they chase, and you may not want their approval. And remember how dunes of sand bury earlier layers: each new event quickly covers the ones before it, and so will your moment of renown be buried.
7.34.today: A viral post is forgotten within days, buried by the next one. And the people whose likes you're refreshing for are usually just as anxious about their own.

7.35.summary:
Marcus copies a passage from Plato's Republic: a person with a large mind who takes in all of time and all of existence can't think a single human life is anything great, and so won't think death is anything bad.

He quotes it because it captures a favourite exercise of his own: zooming out to the scale of the cosmos so that his own life and death shrink to their true proportions.

7.36.summary: A saying of Antisthenes, a follower of Socrates whose ideas fed into the Cynic and Stoic traditions: it is kingly to do good and be badly spoken of. Marcus, an emperor, takes it personally. Being misrepresented is simply part of doing the right thing in public life.
7.36.today: The manager who makes a fair but unpopular call, or the parent who says no and is called mean, is in the same position. Doing right sometimes means accepting that people will grumble.

7.37.summary: It's shameful that your face obeys your mind, putting on whatever expression you choose, while your mind won't order and compose itself. Marcus is pointing at the oddity of controlling your outward look while letting your inner state run wild.
7.37.today: Most of us can smile politely through a tense meeting. The harder, more useful skill is calming the irritation underneath, not just hiding it behind a pleasant face.

7.38.summary:
Here begins a run of quotations Marcus has collected, mostly lines from Greek plays. This one, from Euripides: there's no point being angry with things, because they don't care at all.

He keeps it because it neatly states a Stoic point: events and objects are indifferent to your fury, so anger at them only hurts you.
7.38.today: Swearing at a printer that jams, kicking a flat tyre or glaring at the rain changes nothing in the world. It only changes your mood for the worse.

7.39.summary: A single line, probably a prayer from a play or a hymn, which Marcus jotted down without saying where it came from: may you give joy to the immortal gods and to us. He seems to keep it as a reminder that a good life should please both the gods and one's fellow people.

7.40.summary: From Euripides: life is harvested like ripe ears of corn, one person born, another dying. Marcus treats death as part of a natural cycle, as ordinary and fitting as a harvest. It isn't an outrage, just the turning of the seasons applied to people.

7.41.summary: Another line from Euripides: if the gods neglect me and my children, there is a reason for it. Marcus, who lost several of his children young, keeps it as a way of accepting even the hardest misfortunes as part of an order he may not understand.

7.42.summary: A short line Marcus copied from a Greek play: for the good is with me, and the just. He likely keeps it as a reminder that whatever happens outside, goodness and justice are the possessions no one can take from him.

7.43.summary: A fragment Marcus copied, source unknown: no joining in with other people's wailing, no violent emotion. It's a reminder to himself not to get swept up in the crowd's grief or outrage. That doesn't mean being cold. It means keeping his footing while others lose theirs.
7.43.today: When a group chat spirals into panic about a rumour, or the office joins in moaning about a change, you can stay sympathetic without adding your own voice to the chorus.

7.44.summary:
From Plato's account of Socrates at his trial. Socrates says a person worth anything shouldn't weigh up the risk of living or dying, only whether what they're doing is just or unjust, the act of a good or a bad person.

Marcus quotes it because Socrates was his great example of someone who lived this out: he faced execution rather than abandon what he thought right.

7.45.summary:
More from Socrates' defence speech. Wherever you've taken your stand, because you judged it best or because a commander put you there, you should stay and face the danger, counting neither death nor anything else as worse than the disgrace of deserting your post.

For Marcus, an emperor stuck on the frontier at war, this was not abstract. His post was the empire, and he meant to hold it.
7.45.today: Staying with a hard job because people depend on you, caring for an ailing parent when it would be easier to step back, or speaking up in a meeting when silence would be safer are all versions of holding your post.

7.46.summary:
From Plato's Gorgias, Socrates speaking: what is noble and good may be something quite different from saving lives or being saved. A real person shouldn't fret over how long they'll live or cling to life, but leave that to God, accept the old saying that no one escapes their fate, and ask only how best to live the time they have.

Marcus keeps it because it turns the question from how long to how well.

7.47.summary: Look up at the stars and imagine moving along with them in their courses, and think often about how the elements turn into one another. Marcus says such thoughts wash away the grime of everyday life. It's a deliberate change of perspective, from the petty and local to the vast and orderly.
7.47.today: Ten minutes outside on a clear night, or reading about how far away the nearest galaxy is, can make the morning's argument over the washing-up feel as small as it really is.

7.48.summary:
Marcus quotes a saying he credits to Plato: when you talk about human beings, look at them as if from high above. See their assemblies, armies, farming, weddings, treaties, births and deaths, lawsuits, deserts, foreign peoples, feasts, funerals and markets all at once.

From up there, life looks like a great mixture, yet an ordered combination of opposites. The view from above cools your judgement and reveals the pattern.
7.48.today: Picture your town from a plane window: the school run, a wedding, a hospital ward, a football match, a funeral, all happening at once. Your own worry is one dot in that busy, oddly coherent scene.

7.49.summary: Look back at the great rises and falls of power in history, and you can foresee the future too, because it will follow the same patterns. So watching human life for forty years is as good as watching it for ten thousand. What more would you see? Marcus finds this oddly freeing: you have already seen enough to understand how things go.

7.50.summary:
Marcus quotes lines from Euripides: what grew from the earth returns to the earth, and what sprang from heavenly seed returns to the heavens. Then he adds his own drier gloss.

Death, he says, is either the coming apart of linked atoms or a similar scattering of the elements, which feel nothing. Whichever way you see it, it is a return, not a catastrophe.

7.51.summary:
Two quotations side by side. The first, from Euripides, mocks people who try to dodge death with special diets, drinks and magic, as if diverting a river. The second says we must endure whatever wind heaven sends, and work on without complaint.

Marcus sets them together as a contrast: frantic attempts to escape fate on one side, steady acceptance on the other.
7.51.today: The modern version might be chasing every supplement and anti-ageing fad in the hope of cheating time. The alternative is to look after yourself sensibly, accept what comes and get on with your work.

7.52.summary: Someone else may be better than you at wrestling, but that doesn't make them more sociable, more modest, more ready for whatever life brings, or more patient with their neighbours' faults. Marcus is telling himself that those are the contests worth winning.
7.52.today: A colleague may be sharper at presentations or a friend fitter on the bike. That's fine. Whether you're kinder, steadier and more forgiving is the comparison that actually matters.

7.53.summary: Wherever you can act in line with the reason shared by gods and humans, there's nothing to fear. When you're doing what you're built to do and doing it well, no real harm can come of it. Marcus means that acting rightly is always safe ground, whatever the outcome.

7.54.summary: At every moment you can do three things: accept your present situation with reverence, treat the people around you fairly, and apply care to your current thoughts so that nothing slips in unexamined. Marcus is boiling Stoic practice down to what's always available, here and now.
7.54.today: Stuck in a delayed train, you can still accept the delay, be decent to the stressed guard and notice the irritated thoughts before they take hold. Any moment, however dull, gives you those three jobs.

7.55.summary:
Don't peer at other people's minds; look straight at where nature is leading you, both through what happens to you and through what you must do. Rational beings are made for each other, so the first principle of human nature is to be social.

The second is not to give in to the body's urges, since reason is meant to direct the senses and appetites, not be ruled by them. The third is to avoid error and being deceived. Hold to these and go straight on.
7.55.today: Instead of scrolling through other people's lives to compare, ask what your situation and your role are asking of you. Then: be good to people, don't let cravings make your decisions, and check the facts before you believe the headline.

7.56.summary: Imagine you have already died and your life is complete up to now. Whatever time is left is a bonus, so live it in line with nature. Marcus uses the thought of death to clear away regret and anxiety and make the remainder count.
7.56.today: Treating today as extra time can change how you spend it: less fretting over the email you sent badly yesterday, more attention to the person across the table.

7.57.summary: Love only what happens to you, what is woven into the thread of your fate. What could suit you better? Marcus isn't asking for passive resignation but for embracing your circumstances as genuinely yours, the material your life is made from.

7.58.summary:
Whatever happens, remember everyone it has happened to before: how they fumed, treated it as outrageous, complained, and where they are now. Nowhere. So why copy them? Leave that agitation to those who cause and feel it, and focus on making good use of what happens, treating it as material to work on.

Attend to yourself and aim to be good in every act. The passage breaks off mid-sentence; the end has been lost.
7.58.today: Think of every generation that raged about rising prices, noisy neighbours or new technology. They're gone, and the complaining achieved nothing. The useful question is what you can make of the situation.

7.59.summary: Look inward. The source of goodness is inside you, and it will keep flowing as long as you keep digging. Marcus means that goodness isn't found in outside things; it's something you draw up from your own mind by continual effort.

7.60.summary: The body should be steady and composed in movement and posture, just as the face shows a mind that is intelligent and decent. But Marcus adds an important caveat: this should come without affectation. Outer calm should reflect inner order, not be a performance.

7.61.summary: Living well is more like wrestling than dancing. A dancer follows a known routine; a wrestler has to stand ready and firm for sudden, unexpected attacks. Marcus is telling himself to expect the unplanned rather than assume life will follow the steps.
7.61.today: The day rarely goes to plan: the child gets ill, the server crashes, the boss moves the deadline. Expecting to grapple, not glide, makes those moments less of a shock.

7.62.summary: Keep looking at who the people are whose approval you want, and what guides their thinking. Once you see where their opinions and appetites come from, you won't blame them when they wrong you without meaning to, and you won't want their praise so badly either.
7.62.today: Before you agonise over the opinion of the loudest person in the office or a stranger's comment online, ask what drives their judgements. Often it's habit, envy or their own insecurity, which makes their verdict easier to let go of.

7.63.summary:
Marcus recalls a saying of Plato, "the philosopher": no soul is ever deprived of truth willingly. The same holds for justice, self-control, kindness and every virtue. People who lack them do so out of error, not because they want to be bad.

He says this is essential to keep in mind, because it makes you gentler with everyone.
7.63.today: When a teenager is surly or a stranger is short with you, it can help to assume they don't actually want to be like this. That assumption tends to turn irritation into patience.

7.64.summary:
In any pain, remember that there's no disgrace in it and that it doesn't damage your mind's ability to reason or to get on with people. Marcus borrows from Epicurus, a rival philosopher: pain is neither unbearable nor endless if you remember its limits and don't add to it with imagination.

He also notes that many everyday discomforts, like drowsiness, heat or loss of appetite, are really forms of pain, and grumbling about them is giving in to pain.
7.64.today: Moaning about a sweltering office, a sleepless night or a hunger pang before lunch is the same habit as dreading bigger pains. Noticing the small surrenders helps with the large ones.

7.65.summary: Don't feel towards the people who hate humanity the way they feel towards everyone else. Even when someone behaves inhumanly, Marcus tells himself, answering their hostility with hostility would make him like them.
7.65.today: When someone online is spewing contempt, the temptation is to despise them back. Refusing to catch their attitude, and staying humane towards them, is the harder and better course.

7.66.summary:
Marcus asks how we know Socrates was better than Telauges, a little-known figure, said to be a son of Pythagoras. Socrates' famous feats, such as his noble death, his debating skill, his endurance of a freezing night on campaign and his refusal to help arrest Leon of Salamis for the tyrants of Athens, aren't enough on their own.

What matters is the inner life: whether he was content to be just and pious, unbothered by others' wickedness, unafraid of his lot, and untroubled by the body's sufferings.

7.67.summary:
Your mind isn't so tangled up with your body that you can't govern yourself and keep what's yours in your control. You can be a truly godlike person and have nobody notice. Remember also that a happy life needs very little.

Marcus admits he has given up hope of being a skilled logician or natural scientist, but tells himself that's no reason to give up being free, modest, sociable and obedient to God.
7.67.today: You might never write the novel, run the marathon or get the qualification you once hoped for. That doesn't stop you from being honest, generous and calm, which nobody may notice but which count for more.

7.68.summary:
You can live free and deeply calm even if everyone shouts against you, even if wild beasts tear the body apart. Nothing stops the mind from judging things accurately and using whatever comes its way.

It can say to an event, this is what you really are, whatever people think, and to a circumstance, you're exactly what I was looking for, since everything is material for practising goodness. Nothing that happens is new or unmanageable.

7.69.summary: Good character comes down to three things: living each day as though it might be your last, keeping an even keel (neither frantic nor lazy), and being genuine instead of putting on a front. Thinking about your last day isn't meant to be morbid. It's meant to clear away what doesn't matter.
7.69.today: If today were the last, you probably wouldn't spend the evening doom-scrolling or nursing a grudge from a meeting, and you'd likely say the thing you keep meaning to say to someone you love.

7.70.summary: The gods are immortal and have had to put up with humanity, much of it bad, for an endless stretch of time, yet they aren't annoyed and keep caring for people. You, who will be gone soon, are already tired of putting up with bad people, when you're one of them yourself? Marcus turns the complaint back on himself.
7.70.today: When you catch yourself sighing about how impossible everyone is, from flatmates to fellow drivers, remember how often others have had to be patient with your own off days.

7.71.summary: It's absurd not to escape your own faults, which you can do, while trying to escape other people's, which you can't. Marcus is pointing his effort at the one place it can work: himself.
7.71.today: Changing jobs to get away from a difficult colleague often leads to another difficult colleague. Working on your own impatience, by contrast, pays off wherever you go.

7.72.summary: Your reasoning, social mind is right to consider anything that is neither reasonable nor social as beneath it. Marcus means that you should judge what deserves your respect by the standard of reason and community, not by power, wealth or popularity.

7.73.summary: Once you've done a good deed and someone has benefited, why look for a third thing, either a reputation for kindness or something in return? Marcus says only fools do that. The good act is already complete.
7.73.today: Holding the door, covering a colleague's shift or helping a neighbour with their shopping is finished when it's done. Mentioning it later, or waiting for a thank-you card, adds nothing.

7.74.summary: Nobody gets tired of receiving benefits. Acting according to nature is itself a benefit to you, so don't tire of it when you do good for others. Marcus means that helping people is as good for the helper as for the helped.

7.75.summary:
The nature of the universe once set out to make the world. Now, either everything that happens follows on from that first decision, or even the most important things happen without any guiding purpose.

This echoes Marcus's recurring question of whether the universe is ordered by a purpose or is just chance. He says that remembering it will make you calmer about many things. Either way, events are not aimed at you, and your task stays the same.
